input: The pump affinity laws provide a convenient way of describing how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its speed is varied, and they can be summarised in terms of three straightforward proportionalities. Firstly, the flow varies in direct proportion to the speed: if the speed is increased, the flow increases in the same ratio, and if the speed is reduced, the flow falls correspondingly. Secondly, the head varies with the square of the speed, so the head responds more strongly to a change in speed than the flow does. Thirdly, the power varies with the cube of the speed, which means that the power responds more strongly still. A simple worked check helps to make this concrete: if the speed is doubled, the power is multiplied by 8, which follows directly from the cube proportionality. It is worth bearing in mind that these proportional relationships describe the behaviour of a given pump as its speed changes, and they are most naturally applied when comparing operating points of that pump at different speeds. In practice, this is why relatively modest adjustments to speed can be used to trim the duty of a pump, and why, conversely, a decision to run a pump appreciably faster than its original duty point needs to be examined with some care, since the power absorbed rises so much more steeply than either the flow or the head.
target: Doubling the speed of a centrifugal pump multiplies its power by 8. The affinity laws give the three proportionalities behind that check. Flow is proportional to speed: at twice the speed, the same pump delivers twice the flow, and at half the speed, half the flow. Head is proportional to the square of the speed, and head therefore responds more strongly to a speed change than flow does. Power is proportional to the cube of the speed, and power responds more strongly than head. The worked check follows from the cube proportionality alone: a doubling of speed raises the power by the cube of the speed ratio. Read in the other direction, the same proportionalities give the flow, head, and power at a reduced speed from the values at the original speed, with the power falling fastest as speed is reduced. The three proportionalities are not three separate rules: they are one similarity statement read for three quantities, and the steepening from flow to head to power is the content of the laws. A speed change that looks modest against flow is therefore not modest against power, and the check case is the extreme form of that difference. The laws compare operating points of a given centrifugal pump at varying speed. Each proportionality is a ratio statement between two speeds of that pump, and the three statements together fix how flow, head, and power move when the speed is set to a new value.
